theme: Seeing a doctor and taking sick leave
summary_zh: 學會向醫生描述症狀、聽懂醫囑，並用 have to／be supposed to／had better 跟主管和同事說明請假與交接。

vocab.example: I'm a bit under the weather, so I'll join the meeting by video.
vocab.example_zh: 我身體有點不舒服，所以會用視訊參加會議。

vocab.definition: to have a body temperature that is higher than normal
vocab.example: My son has been running a fever since last night.
vocab.example_zh: 我兒子從昨晚開始一直發燒。

vocab.definition: a sign that you have an illness, such as a cough or a headache
vocab.example: Tell the doctor about all your symptoms, even the small ones.
vocab.example_zh: 把所有症狀都告訴醫生，就算是小症狀也要說。

vocab.definition: a doctor's written order for medicine, or the medicine itself
vocab.example: You can pick up your prescription at the pharmacy downstairs.
vocab.example_zh: 你可以到樓下的藥局領處方藥。

vocab.definition: to stay away from work for a period
vocab.example: You should take time off until you feel better.
vocab.example_zh: 你應該請假到身體好一點再說。

vocab.definition: to become very tired and unable to work well because you have worked too hard
vocab.example: If you keep working until midnight, you'll burn out.
vocab.example_zh: 如果你一直工作到半夜，會把自己累垮。

vocab.definition: a note from a doctor that says you were too sick to work
vocab.example: HR needs a doctor's note if you're out for more than three days.
vocab.example_zh: 如果請病假超過三天，人資需要診斷證明。

vocab.definition: to rest so that you get your energy back
vocab.example: Rest up this weekend so you're ready for Monday.
vocab.example_zh: 這個週末好好休養，星期一才有精神。

reading.title: The Week I Finally Listened to My Body
paragraphs: For most of October, I'd been getting by on four or five hours of sleep. Our team was falling behind on a big client project, and I kept telling myself I just had to get through one more week. Then, on a Tuesday morning, I woke up feeling under the weather, and it got worse fast: a sore throat, a headache, and a fever that kept climbing.

I was supposed to present to the client that afternoon, so my first instinct was to take some medicine and get on the train anyway. My commute is almost an hour, though, and by the time I'd made coffee, I could barely stand. I texted my manager, Grace, to give her a heads-up, and she replied right away: "You'd better stay home. Jun can cover the presentation."

At the clinic, the doctor confirmed that I was running a fever of 38.5°C and asked about my other symptoms. When I mentioned how many late nights I'd been working, she looked at me over her glasses. "You don't have to be a hero," she said. "If you keep this up, you're going to burn out." She gave me a prescription and a doctor's note, and told me to rest up for at least three days.

Deciding to take time off felt strange at first. But Jun handled the presentation well, the client signed off on the plan, and the project is back on track. When I got back, it only took me a morning to get up to speed. Grace also suggested that we keep a shortlist of backup presenters for every big meeting, so one sick person doesn't put a whole project at risk.
I sent Jun a thank-you message: "I owe you one." He wrote back, "Just don't make me do it again next week!"

questions.q: Why did the writer stay home on Tuesday?
options: Her doctor called and told her not to come in.
Her manager told her to stay home after she sent a message.
The client had canceled the presentation.
questions.explain_zh: 第 2 段：她傳訊息給主管 Grace 先打聲招呼，Grace 馬上回「You'd better stay home.」。她是之後才去看醫生的。

questions.q: Who gave the presentation to the client?
questions.explain_zh: 第 2 段 Grace 說「Jun can cover the presentation」，第 4 段也說「Jun handled the presentation well」。

questions.q: What does the doctor suggest when she says, "You don't have to be a hero"?
options: The writer should work even harder.
The writer had been pushing herself too hard.
The writer's illness was very serious.
The doctor did not believe the writer was sick.
questions.explain_zh: 推論題。醫生是在聽到她熬了很多夜之後才這樣說，接著又說再這樣下去會 burn out，表示她一直太勉強自己。

grammar.point: Modals of obligation and advice: have to, be supposed to, had better
grammar.point_zh: 表示義務與建議：have to、be supposed to、had better

guide.key_zh: 非做不可用 have to；照安排應該用 be supposed to（過去式常指沒做到）；警告用 had better

uses.note_zh: don't have to = 不必，不是「不可以」

uses.label_zh: 照安排或規定應該要（過去式常表示沒做到）
uses.form: S + be + supposed to + V（原形）
uses.note_zh: 過去的約定用 was/were supposed to
口語縮寫 you'd better，後面不加 to；語氣強，像警告，對上司或客戶少用

mistakes.wrong: You had better to stay home.
mistakes.why_zh: had better 後面直接接原形動詞，不加 to

mistakes.wrong: She have to see a doctor.
mistakes.right: She has to see a doctor.
mistakes.why_zh: 主詞是 she（單數）要用 has to

mistakes.wrong: I'm supposed to finish it yesterday.
mistakes.right: I was supposed to finish it yesterday.
mistakes.why_zh: 過去的約定要用 was supposed to

examples.en: You have to take these pills twice a day, with food.
examples.zh: 這些藥一天要吃兩次，要配餐吃。

examples.en: It's just a cold, so you don't have to see a doctor.
examples.zh: 只是感冒而已，你不必去看醫生。

examples.en: I was supposed to present at ten, but I called in sick.
examples.zh: 我本來十點要簡報，但我請了病假。

examples.en: You'd better stay home, or the whole team will catch it.
examples.zh: 你最好待在家，不然全組都會被傳染。

exercises.q: My manager ___ (have to) approve any sick leave longer than three days.
exercises.explain_zh: 這是公司規定 → have to。主詞 my manager 是單數，要用 has to。

exercises.q: You look terrible. You'd better ___ (go) home before it gets worse.
exercises.explain_zh: had better（'d better）後面直接接原形動詞，不加 to：You'd better go。

exercises.q: Tom ___ (be supposed to) send me the slides last night, but he forgot.
exercises.explain_zh: 原本的安排是昨晚（過去），而且沒做到 → was supposed to。

exercises.q: The clinic is open until nine, so you ___ (not / have to) leave work early.
exercises.explain_zh: don't have to = 不必、沒有必要。診所開到九點，所以不需要提早下班，不是「不可以」提早下班。

exercises.q: The sign at the clinic says that all patients ___ check in at the front desk first.
exercises.explain_zh: 診所的規定 → have to；主詞 all patients 是複數，用 have to。had better 後面不加 to；supposing 不是正確形式。

exercises.q: According to the contract, we ___ get the budget approved by last Friday, but the client still hasn't replied.
exercises.explain_zh: 合約約定（安排）的期限是上週五（過去），而且沒做到 → were supposed to。had better 只用在現在或未來的建議，不能講過去；have to 時態不對；supposing 不是正確形式。

review.point: Present perfect continuous for ongoing situations
review.point_zh: 現在完成進行式：從過去持續到現在的狀況

exercises.q: I ___ (cough) since Monday, and it's getting worse.
exercises.explain_zh: since Monday 一直到現在還在咳 → have been + V-ing。

exercises.q: My throat ___ (hurt) on and off all week.
exercises.explain_zh: all week 斷斷續續一直到現在 → 現在完成進行式。主詞 my throat 是單數，用 has been hurting（不是 have been hurt）。

exercises.q: "How long ___ this headache?" the doctor asked.
exercises.explain_zh: 頭痛從過去持續到現在 → How long + 現在完成式。have 在這裡是「有（頭痛）」，屬於狀態動詞，通常不用進行式，所以用 have you had，而不是 have you been having。did you have 表示已經結束；are you having／do you have 不能和 How long 搭配表示「到現在多久了」。

guide.key_zh: 從過去開始、到現在還在持續的事，用 have/has been + V-ing

uses.label_zh: 從過去一直持續到現在（還在進行）
uses.signal: for two weeks, since August, lately, all day

uses.label_zh: 看到現在的樣子，推測剛剛一直在做什麼

mistakes.wrong: I've been seeing three apartments this week.
mistakes.right: I've seen three apartments this week.
mistakes.why_zh: 講次數、結果用現在完成式，不用進行式

mistakes.wrong: I've been knowing him for years.
mistakes.why_zh: know、like、own 這類狀態動詞通常不用進行式

mistakes.wrong: I've been working here since three years.
mistakes.right: I've been working here for three years.
mistakes.why_zh: for 接一段時間，since 接開始的時間點

timeline.label: I've been looking for an apartment since August.
I saw one yesterday.
timeline.note_zh: 對照：過去式，一個時間點

listening.title: At the Clinic

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Emily
lines.text: Hi, Dr. Patel. I've been coughing since Sunday, and now I'm running a fever.

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Dr. Patel
lines.text: I'm sorry to hear that. Have you been taking anything for it?

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Emily
lines.text: Just some cold medicine. I'm supposed to fly to Singapore on Thursday for a client meeting, so I really need to get better fast.

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Dr. Patel
lines.text: Let's take a look. Your throat is quite red, and your temperature is 38.4°C. It looks like a throat infection. I'm afraid you'd better not fly this week.

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Emily
lines.text: Seriously? My manager, Linda, booked the trip a month ago. She's going to be so upset.

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Dr. Patel
lines.text: I can write you a doctor's note. You don't have to explain everything to her yourself.

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Emily
lines.text: That would help. My colleague Tom could probably go instead. He'd only need a day to get up to speed.

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Dr. Patel
lines.text: That sounds like a good plan. Now, you have to take these antibiotics twice a day, with food, until they're finished.

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Emily
lines.text: Even if I feel better after two days?

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Dr. Patel
lines.text: Yes, that's important. And come back on Monday if the cough hasn't cleared up.

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Emily
lines.text: Okay. Thanks, Doctor. I'll text Linda to give her a heads-up right now.

questions.q: Who booked Emily's trip to Singapore?
questions.explain_zh: Emily 說：「My manager, Linda, booked the trip a month ago.」訂行程的是主管 Linda；Tom 是可能代替她出差的同事。

questions.q: What does Dr. Patel say about the antibiotics?
options: Emily can stop taking them when she feels better.
Emily has to take them twice a day with food until they're finished.
Emily should only take them before she flies.
Emily should take them once a day before bed.
questions.explain_zh: 醫生說：「you have to take these antibiotics twice a day, with food, until they're finished」，Emily 問好了可不可以停，醫生說不行。

questions.q: How does Emily most likely feel when the doctor tells her not to fly?
options: Disappointed and worried about how her manager will react
questions.explain_zh: 推論題。她說「Seriously?」，又說主管 Linda「is going to be so upset」，可見她很失望，也擔心主管的反應。

dictation: I've been coughing since Sunday, and now I'm running a fever.
He'd only need a day to get up to speed.
I can write you a doctor's note.

shadowing: I'm afraid you'd better not fly this week.
You don't have to explain everything to her yourself.
He'd only need a day to get up to speed.

prompts.question: Your 3 p.m. meeting is running over, but you're seeing the doctor at 4:30. Tell the team in one sentence.
prompts.question_zh: 下午三點的會議超時了，但你四點半已經約好看醫生。用一句話告訴大家（打字或小聲說都可以）。
prompts.sample: Sorry, I have to leave now because I'm seeing the doctor at 4:30.

prompts.question: A coworker in your meeting keeps coughing and looks tired. Make one suggestion in one or two sentences.
prompts.question_zh: 會議中有位同事一直咳嗽、看起來很累。用一兩句話給他一個建議。
prompts.sample: You don't look well. I'd suggest that you go home and rest, and I can send you the notes.

writing.task: You are sick and can't go to tomorrow's team meeting, where you were going to present. Write an email of 80-150 words to your manager, Linda. Say what's wrong, what you were supposed to do tomorrow, who could cover for you, and when you'll be back.
writing.task_zh: 你生病了，無法參加明天原本要上台簡報的團隊會議。寫一封 80–150 個英文字的 email 給主管 Linda：說明身體狀況、你明天原本要做什麼、誰可以代替你，以及你什麼時候回來。
writing.sample:
Hi Linda,

Just a quick heads-up: I came down with a throat infection over the weekend, and the doctor has told me to rest at home until Wednesday. I've attached my doctor's note.

I'm supposed to present the Q4 budget at tomorrow's team meeting. I'd suggest that Tom present it instead. He has already seen the slides, so he won't have to prepare much. I'll send him my notes this afternoon.

I'm seeing the doctor again on Wednesday morning, and I expect to be back on Thursday. I'll let you know how it goes. Sorry for the short notice.

Best,
Emily
checklist_zh: 開頭先用 heads-up 簡短說明狀況
用 supposed to 說明原本的安排
用 I'd suggest that + 主詞 + 原形動詞 提出代理人
已經排好的看診用 I'm seeing the doctor…（現在進行式）

translation.zh: 我建議我們把會議改到下週一。
translation.en: I'd suggest that we move the meeting to next Monday.
alt: I'd suggest moving the meeting to next Monday.

translation.zh: 我們要不要先請 Tom 準備簡報？
translation.en: Why don't we ask Tom to prepare the presentation first?
alt: Why don't we ask Tom to get the presentation ready first?

translation.zh: 我已經排好明天下午三點看醫生了。
translation.en: I'm seeing the doctor at 3 p.m. tomorrow.
alt: I'm seeing the doctor tomorrow at 3 p.m.
I'm seeing a doctor at 3 p.m. tomorrow.

translation.zh: 你看起來很不舒服，最好今天早點回家。
translation.en: You don't look well. You'd better go home early today.
alt: You look sick. You'd better go home early today.
You don't look well. You had better go home early today.

reading.title: The Hidden Cost of Showing Up Sick
paragraphs: In many offices, dragging yourself in with a fever is still quietly admired. The colleague who powers through a cold, tissues piled on the desk, is seen as dedicated; the one who calls in sick is suspected, at least privately, of taking it easy. Researchers have a name for this habit: presenteeism.

The problem is that presenteeism is expensive. Several studies have suggested that the productivity lost when people work while ill outweighs the cost of the days they take off. Someone running a fever is slower, more prone to mistakes, and, of course, likely to pass the illness on. One sick employee in an open-plan office can take out half a team within a week.

So why do people keep doing it? Partly it's workload. If nobody is going to cover for you, staying home simply means the work piles up until you get back. Partly it's culture. When managers praise the person who "never misses a day," they are sending a message, whether they intend to or not, about what the company really values.

Some firms have started tackling the issue head-on. Rather than leaving it to individual judgment, they spell out when staff are expected to stay home, and they make sure every key task has a named backup. Managers are encouraged to set an example themselves; a director who logs off when she's ill makes it far easier for a junior employee to do the same.

None of this means people should disappear at the first sniffle. But the old assumption that showing up is always the responsible choice is starting to look outdated. More often than not, the responsible choice is the one that keeps everyone else healthy, too.

questions.q: According to the first paragraph, how are people who call in sick sometimes seen?
options: As possibly not really ill and just taking it easy
questions.explain_zh: 第 1 段：請病假的人「is suspected, at least privately, of taking it easy」，被私下懷疑只是想偷懶。

questions.q: Which reason for presenteeism does the writer give?
options: People enjoy being in the office.
Work piles up when nobody covers for you.
Doctors often advise people to keep working.
Sick days are not allowed by law.
questions.explain_zh: 第 3 段：「If nobody is going to cover for you, staying home simply means the work piles up」。

questions.q: What does the writer imply about managers?
options: Their own behavior strongly affects what employees feel they can do.
They should never take sick days.
They can do nothing about presenteeism.
They are the main reason illnesses spread.
questions.explain_zh: 推論題。第 3 段說主管稱讚「從不請假」的人就是在傳達訊息，第 4 段說主管自己生病就下線，員工也比較敢這麼做，可見主管的行為影響很大。

listening.title: Go Home, Kevin

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Hannah
lines.text: Kevin? What are you doing here? You sound awful.

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Kevin
lines.text: I'm fine, honestly. It's just a cold. I've got the quarterly review at two, and—

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Hannah
lines.text: And you're going to cough all over the leadership team? Come on.

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Kevin
lines.text: Look, if I don't present, who will? Nobody else has been working on those numbers.

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Hannah
lines.text: Priya has. She's been sitting in on every budget call since September.

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Kevin
lines.text: Yeah, but she'd have to get up to speed on the forecast, and that's, what, two hours of work?

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Hannah
lines.text: Which is still less than the three days you'll be out if this gets worse. Seriously, you'd better go home.

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Kevin
lines.text: Ugh. Okay, but if Mark asks why I bailed, I'm blaming you.

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Hannah
lines.text: Deal. I'll tell him you're contagious and that he should be thanking me.

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Kevin
lines.text: Fine. I'll send Priya the deck and walk her through it on a call.

lines.speaker: A
lines.name: Hannah
lines.text: From your couch. With soup.

lines.speaker: B
lines.name: Kevin
lines.text: With soup. Got it. I owe you one, Hannah.

questions.q: Who has been joining the budget calls since September?
questions.explain_zh: Hannah 說：「Priya has. She's been sitting in on every budget call since September.」

questions.q: Why does Hannah think Kevin should go home?
options: He hasn't prepared for the review.
Getting sicker would cost more time than Priya needs to prepare.
Priya wants to give the presentation.
questions.explain_zh: 推論題。Kevin 說 Priya 要花兩小時準備，Hannah 回答那還是比他病情加重、請三天假少，意思是硬撐的代價更大。

questions.q: What does Kevin mean when he says, "If Mark asks why I bailed, I'm blaming you"?
options: He is jokingly agreeing to leave.
He plans to complain to Mark about Hannah.
questions.explain_zh: 推論題。他先說 Okay，接著半開玩笑說要怪 Hannah，表示他其實同意回家了。bail 是口語的「落跑、臨時退出」。

dictation: Nobody else has been working on those numbers.
She's been sitting in on every budget call since September.

glossary.definition: going to work when you are ill and cannot work well
to be greater or more important than something else
likely to do or suffer from something bad
to explain something clearly and in detail
to attend a meeting without being a main member of it
to leave or stop doing something suddenly
